In 2001, three films challenged familiar conventions of Hindi-language cinema in very different ways.

	Farhan Akhtar‘s “Dil Chahta Hai” offered a new screen language for friendship and young adulthood; Ashutosh Gowariker‘s “Lagaan” turned a village cricket match into an epic about resistance; and Madhur Bhandarkar’s “Chandni Bar” took audiences into the largely unseen world of Mumbai’s dance bars. Twenty-five years later, the filmmakers revisited the films and the risks behind them at “The Legendary 25s,” a session at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa moderated by actor and producer Khushboo Sundar.
	

	One thread connected their stories: all three had encountered the expectations of commercial Hindi cinema before finding the conviction to make something different.

	Gowariker and Bhandarkar already had films behind them before “Lagaan” and “Chandni Bar” established their identities as filmmakers. Akhtar, making his directorial debut with “Dil Chahta Hai,” said he had not been interested in making a film that conformed to the prevailing Bollywood potboiler template.

	For Gowariker, who is also the IFFI festival director this year, the turning point came after his first two films failed. Having initially tried to make commercial entertainers, he realized that “my next film had to be something I believe in, something that I want to make first, and then hope to God that the audience also likes it. So that’s how the genesis of ‘Lagaan’ happened.”

	The idea was an unlikely proposition: a period drama built around a cricket match, with villagers taking on the British. Gowariker wanted to make a film about “a group of heroes.” He researched the British Raj, 19th-century life, cricket and village communities before taking the script back to star Aamir Khan, who had initially rejected the premise. Gowariker asked Khan for just three hours to hear the narration of “Lagaan” before deciding. “He heard it. He laughed, he had tears and he said, ‘I definitely want to do this now,'” Gowariker recalled of the film, which went on to receive an Oscar nomination.
	

	Bhandarkar’s route to “Chandni Bar” was rooted in observation. A visit to a dance bar with a friend gave him the subject for the Tabu-starring film, which he researched by visiting bars across Mumbai for six months. “Even if, in retrospect, ‘Chandni Bar’ had not done well at the box office, I would still be happy because this is the cinema which I wanted to make, and this is the world which I’ve seen,” he said.

	His interest in underdogs has continued in films such as “Page 3,” “Corporate” and “Fashion,” which examined the worlds of the media, business and fashion respectively. He has also resisted pressure to turn women-centered stories into male-led films for commercial reasons. From Tabu’s vulnerable character in “Chandni Bar” to Raveena Tandon’s politically ambitious woman in “Satta,” he said he is drawn to complex women rather than idealized portrayals. “My movies are basically a mirror to society,” he said.

	With “Dil Chahta Hai,” a buddy movie starring Aamir Khan, Saif Ali Khan and Akshaye Khanna, Akhtar set out to bring a more recognizable version of friendship to the screen. He felt Hindi films’ depictions of male friendship did not reflect how people actually spent time together. “The relationship had become cheesy, filmy,” he said. He cited Mansoor Khan’s “Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak” (1988), which he watched as a schoolboy, as an important influence.

	Asked specifically about the older-woman romance in “Dil Chahta Hai,” he said the inspiration for the relationship between the characters played by Akshaye Khanna and Dimple Kapadia came “from many crushes that I had on older women, that’s the honest truth.”

	The filmmakers also reflected on how cinema is made and judged. Akhtar described a screenplay as “a living, breathing thing,” evolving through contributions from actors and crew members, sometimes well into the edit. Gowariker, discussing acting, said, “The true performance lies in the pauses where you’re not saying anything.”

	On the industry’s fixation with box-office numbers, Akhtar said, “Now the conversation is that I heard you had a great weekend. But I would rather know what you thought of the film.” Gowariker described every new film as “a reset to zero,” adding that the yardsticks had shifted over the years, from silver and golden jubilees to 100-day runs and opening weekends, making comparisons across films of different budgets and genres reductive.
	

	Asked what they would change if they could revisit one another’s films, Akhtar said he would leave “Lagaan” untouched, but if he were the producer, he would ask Gowariker to direct it again. Gowariker said he might add a soulful song to “Chandni Bar,” while Bhandarkar said he would find it difficult to remake either “Lagaan” or “Dil Chahta Hai.”

	On AI and visual effects, Bhandarkar said, “AI and VFX can certainly enhance the visual experience and expand the possibilities of filmmaking, but they can never replace the human touch.” Akhtar’s advice to younger filmmakers was to draw on their own unique experiences.

title: NBC Pulls Spot Advocating for End of U.S. Military Aid to Israel, Will Review Approval Procedures After Outcry
description: NBC has pulled an ad from a Middle East advocacy organization that calls for the end of U.S. military aid to Israel. The network will review its ad
body:
NBC has pulled an ad from a Middle East advocacy organization that calls for the end of U.S. military aid to Israel. The network will review its ad approval procedures after criticism from the Simon Wiesenthal Center and other organizations.

	The spot, purchased by the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, pushes for the end of U.S. military aid to Israel amid the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. The spot titled “Every Three Seconds” ran Nov. 25 on NBC in primetime during the network’s “Saturday Night Live” Thanksgiving special.
	

	The ad makes a jarring juxtaposition between the suffering in Gaza and scenes of a typical American preteen girl doing chores and odd jobs to save money for a bicycle amid tough economic times. Just as the American girl brings her jar full of money into a bike shop, the spot cuts to a scene of a girl standing in a pile of rubble in Gaza. As the camera pans back, the girl is revealed to be leaning on a crutch, having lost one of her lower legs. The spot tells viewers that “Every three seconds” the U.S. sends about $400 million in military aid to Israel under a long-term deal set to expire in 2028.

	NBC’s top brass were unaware of the spot before it aired. As a result, there will be a review of the network’s ad approval processes, according to a person familiar with the situation.

	Jim Berk, CEO of the Wiesenthal Center, issued a lengthy statement on Thursday questioning NBC’s decision to air the ad during an “SNL” entertainment special in primetime. He pointed to the ad’s potential to fuel hostility against Israel and Jews.
	

	“The advertisement’s imagery, an American child’s hardship set against the anguish of a child in Gaza, offers viewers a seductive but unsubstantiated narrative: that the struggles of American families are somehow bound up with U.S. support for Israel,” Berk stated. “In collapsing a complex foreign policy into a single, emotionally charged image, it erases the deeper realities, including the imperative to protect Israeli lives and the very existence of the country itself. By manipulating emotion and stripping it of context, this ad seeks to become a catalyst for hostility. … Without scrutiny, insinuations and half-truths are allowed to seep into the consciousness of millions, unchallenged and unchecked. Turning children’s suffering into a prop for political theater is an unacceptable manipulation.”

	The Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project did not immediately respond to a request for comment on NBC’s decision. It’s unclear how many more times the spot had been scheduled to run on NBCUniversal platforms. According to the organization’s website, IMEU “was founded in 2005 by a group of concerned Americans who want to foster an increased understanding among Americans about Palestine and the Palestinians.”

Nov 27, 2026 3:10pm PT	
	

			


			
			
	

									A24
	

		
	
				

	The starting gun of the Oscar season starts Monday, and by next Sunday, it will have a shape that many of us will be able to see clearly.

	For months, the Oscar race has run on festival premieres, studio screenings and ever more elaborate predictions, mine included. This week, the people with ballots finally speak.

	The Gothams, the New York Film Critics Circle, the National Board of Review, the American Film Institute and LAFCA each answer to a different electorate and each has its own complicated history with the Academy. None of them pick the Oscars, but they all shape the conversation that follows.

	The question isn’t only who wins. It’s who wins where, and what each victory says about the corner of the electorate that handed it out.

	Here’s what’s on the calendar this week.

	Monday, Nov. 30: Gotham AwardsTuesday, Dec. 1: New York Film Critics Circle AwardsWednesday, Dec. 2: Film Independent Spirit Awards nominationsWednesday, Dec. 2: National Board of Review AwardsThursday, Dec. 3: AFI Awards honorees announcedFriday, Dec. 4: Critics Choice Awards nominationsFriday, Dec. 4: BAFTA Round One voting opensFriday, Dec. 4: Golden Globes nomination voting endsSunday, Dec. 6: British Independent Film AwardsSunday, Dec. 6: Los Angeles Film Critics Association Awards announcement

	Here’s how we see the opening week unfolding, with some commentary for each.


			
			
	Gotham Awards (Nov. 30)
			
										
					Image Credit: A24				
					
				

	The Gothams have long been a launching pad for independent cinema, a place for films that might otherwise get flattened by the studio machine. In 2023, the organization scrapped its $35 million budget ceiling and opened more categories to international titles. The result is a more eclectic ballot, one that puts established auteurs and first-time filmmakers side by side. This year, that means 42 features and 25 performances across 11 categories.

	That makes the Gothams a natural first stop for “The Invite,” which we expect to win best feature. Wilde’s ensemble piece, starring Seth Rogen, Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton, has the kind of dinner-party-argument appeal that plays well with this voting body. “Josephine” is my alternate and could follow some jaw-dropping selections like “A Different Man” two years ago. The drama took both the U.S. Grand Jury Prize and the Audience Award at Sundance in January, and the Gothams have never lost their appetite for championing a discovery.

	Notably, a different set of industry professionals, five jury members each, for each category, pick the Gotham winners, while Gotham members vote on the audience award. A film can win a jury on artistic grounds while another finds its people in the wider membership.

	Best Feature: “The Invite” (A24)Alternate: “Josephine” (Sumerian Pictures)

	Director: Ryusuke Hamaguchi, “All of a Sudden” (Neon)Alternate: Mike Leigh, “Tender Loving Care” (Bleecker Street)

	Lead Performance: Andrew Scott, “Elsinore” (Focus Features)Alternate: John Malkovich, “Wild Horse Nine” (Searchlight Pictures)

	Supporting Performance: Tao Okamoto, “All of a Sudden” (Neon)Alternate: Kate O’Flynn, “Tender Loving Care” (Bleecker Street)

	Breakthrough Performer: Guitarricadelafuente, “La Bola Negra” (Netflix)Alternate: Adia, “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” (Amazon MGM Studios)

	Audience Award: “You Can See Everything” (A24)Alternate: “La Bola Negra” (Netflix)

	Breakthrough Director: Jordan Firstman, “Club Kid” (A24)Alternate: Aleshea Harris, “Is God Is” (Amazon MGM Studios)

	Original Screenplay: “Tender Loving Care” (Bleecker Street) — Mike LeighAlternate: “Wild Horse Nine” (Searchlight Pictures) — Martin McDonagh

	International Feature: “Possible Love” (Netflix)Alternate: “Blue Heron” (Janus Films)

		
			
			
	New York Film Critics Circle (Dec. 1)
			
										
					Image Credit: A24				
					
				

	Founded in 1935, the New York Film Critics Circle is the country’s oldest film critics organization and one of the most influential early stops on the calendar. Its history is full of choices that challenged the Academy’s conventional wisdom. Many of them went on to become landmarks, even when they diverged from the eventual Oscar winner.

	This year, we’re predicting “You Can See Everything” to show its strength by winning the top prize for best film, with “The Odyssey” as the alternate. Fielder and Oppenheim’s 174-minute portrait of Elizabeth Holmes premiered as Telluride’s secret screening and has drawn the kind of critical fervor usually reserved for narrative features. A best film win from New York wouldn’t automatically make it an Oscar best picture contender, but it would move the film into a different tier of consideration. “The Odyssey” is the more traditional choice: a major filmmaker, a sweeping production and a likely force in the technical categories.

	In directing, Wilde could pull off a deserved citation ahead of Nolan, who has never won from the group before.

	Andrew Scott is my choice for actor, with Robert Pattinson’s combined work in “Primetime” and “The Drama” as the alternate. Julianne Moore could win actress for “The Debut,” with Sandra Hüller for “Rose” as a real threat. In supporting actor, Guitarricadelafuente could keep building momentum for “La Bola Negra,” with a surprise citation for someone like John Cho of “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” (much like Regina Hall or Tiffany Haddish surprised in their respective years). Kate O’Flynn (“Tender Loving Care”) and Amanda Seyfried (“You Can See Everything”) could be in a battle for supporting actress, or someone else completely. 

	The screenplay prize could go to Jordan Firstman for “Club Kid,” with Cristian Mungiu’s “Fjord” as the alternate. “Tangles” is my animated film pick over Laika’s “Wildwood,” an interesting split between independent animation and a more established studio shop.

	Best Film: “You Can See Everything” (A24)Alternate: “The Odyssey” (Universal Pictures)

	Director: Olivia Wilde, “The Invite” (A24)Alternate: Christopher Nolan, “The Odyssey” (Universal Pictures)

	Actor: Andrew Scott, “Elsinore” (Focus Features)Alternate: Robert Pattinson, “Primetime” and “The Drama” (A24)

	Actress: Julianne Moore, “The Debut” (A24)Alternate: Sandra Hüller, “Rose” (Mubi)

	Supporting Actor: Guitarricadelafuente, “La Bola Negra” (Netflix)Alternate: John Cho, “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” (Amazon MGM Studios)

	Supporting Actress: Kate O’Flynn, “Tender Loving Care” (Bleecker Street)Alternate: Amanda Seyfried, “You Can See Everything” (A24)

	Screenplay: “Club Kid” (A24) — Jordan FirstmanAlternate: “Fjord” (Neon) — Cristian Mungiu

	Animated Film: “Tangles” (Independent Film Company)Alternate: “Wildwood” (Laika)

	Cinematography: “Project Hail Mary” (Amazon MGM Studios) — Greig FraserAlternate: “La Bola Negra” (Netflix) — Gris Jordana

	Nonfiction Film: “Rehearsals for a Revolution” (Sony Pictures Classics)Alternate: “Naza” (The Guardian, MK2 and Neon)

	First Film: “Club Kid” (A24) — Jordan FirstmanAlternate: “Obsession” (Focus Features) — Curry Barker

		
			
			
	National Board of Review (Dec. 2)
			
										
					Image Credit: Jonathan Olley				
					
				

	Founded in 1909, the National Board of Review has named a Top 10 every year since 1929. Unlike the critics’ groups, it’s made up of New York-area film enthusiasts rather than working critics. Its selections land just as studios are deciding which campaigns deserve more fuel, which makes it one of the earliest industry signals of the season.

	Variety is predicting “Project Hail Mary” for best film, with “Artificial” as the alternate. That would be a fitting choice for a group that has long rewarded accessible, ambitious filmmaking. Phil Lord and Christopher Miller could also take director, ahead of Denis Villeneuve for “Dune: Part Three.” That would follow the three-year current trend of the same film winning both prizes.

	If both happen, “Project Hail Mary” has an instant entry for best picture.

	The acting picks could be just as revealing, but they don’t always match up with Oscars, so you have to consciously pick an acting winner that probably won’t translate (i.e., Elle Fanning in “A Complete Unknown” or Will Forte in “Nebraska”). Seth Rogen is my actor prediction for “The Invite,” with Matt Damon for “The Odyssey” as the alternate. Inde Navarrette could win actress for “Obsession,” although she can win breakthrough performer. Rachel Zegler won best actress for “West Side Story” (2021) instead of breakthrough her respective year.

	John Leguizamo could follow veteran winners who tend to win supporting actor with “The Odyssey.” A “no guts-no glory” pick exists with Elizabeth Debicki could taking supporting actress for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” with Samantha Morton for “The Odyssey” projected as the runner-up.

	The screenplay categories offer openings for two very different films. James Gray could win original screenplay for “Paper Tiger,” ahead of Curry Barker for “Obsession.” In adapted, Sian Heder and Rebekah Taussig could be recognized for “Being Heumann,” with “La Bola Negra” as the alternate.

	The specialty awards could be telling, too. I’m predicting “Wildwood” for animated feature, Anthony Ippolito for breakthrough performance in “I Play Rocky” and Barker for directorial debut with “Obsession.” “La Bola Negra” could win international film, while “You Can See Everything” is my documentary pick. Hoyte van Hoytema could take cinematography for “The Odyssey,” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” could win stunt artistry. “Naza” is my choice for the NBR Freedom of Expression Award.

	The lists may matter as much as the prizes. For the Top 10, look for glaring omissions but don’t put too much stock in them. “The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King” (2003) settled for the NBR’s ensemble prize without a Top 10 slot, and Guillermo del Toro’s “The Shape of Water” (2017) was left off entirely. Both won best picture. The NBR’s lists are an early endorsement, not a verdict.

	AFI Awards (Dec. 3)
			
										
					Image Credit: Glen Wilson/Lionsgate				
					
				

	The American Film Institute’s annual selections live in a different space from the critics’ prizes. There are no individual performances and no craft citations, just 10 films the institute considers culturally and artistically representative of the year. The Top 10 is restricted to American productions. Works that fall outside its criteria can receive an AFI Special Award, as Kenneth Branagh’s “Belfast” and Questlove’s documentary “Summer of Soul” did in 2021 and Jafar Panahi’s “It Was Just an Accident” did last year.

	That makes the AFI list a measure of which films have entered the industry’s broader conversation. There’s no single winner, and because the list is alphabetical, it isn’t a ranking.

	We’re thinking: “Artificial,” “Dune: Part Three,” “Elsinore,” “I Play Rocky,” “The Invite,” “Michael,” “The Odyssey,” “Project Hail Mary,” “Wild Horse Nine” and “Wildwood.” “Obsession” is my alternate.

	“You Can See Everything” is my Special Award prediction, with “La Bola Negra” as the alternative since neither can win.

	Los Angeles Film Critics Association (Dec. 6)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				

	Founded in 1975 by critics working in print, radio and television, LAFCA has become one of the most respected critics’ groups in the country. It votes and announces in December, then presents its awards at a ceremony in January.

	We’re seeing “The Odyssey” for best film, with “You Can See Everything” as the alternate. That would hand Nolan a major critical endorsement in a week when New York may have gone the other way. That’s exactly why the opening stretch matters: different groups can watch the same year of movies and come away with very different pictures.

	For director, I’m going with Andrey Zvyagintsev for “Minotaur,” ahead of Ryusuke Hamaguchi for “All of a Sudden.”

	With non-gendered acting categories, the group chooses two lead and two supporting performances.

	Lead performance could produce one of the more distinctive outcomes of the season, with Jeon Do-yeon for “Possible Love” and John Malkovich for “Wild Horse Nine” sharing the prize. Virginie Efira for “All of a Sudden” and Andrew Scott for “Elsinore” are the alternatives.

	In supporting performance, Andrew Garfield could win for “Artificial” alongside Amanda Seyfried for “You Can See Everything.” Penélope Cruz for “The Invite” and Anne Hathaway for “The Odyssey” are the alternate selections.

	The screenplay award could go to Jones and McCormack for “The Invite,” with Firstman’s “Club Kid” as the alternative. Add it up: a Gotham best feature, a possible New York director win and an LAFCA screenplay prize would give “The Invite” a broad critical footprint before the guilds have said a word.

	On the craft side, I’m predicting Linus Sandgren for cinematography for “Dune: Part Three,” Adam Locke-Norton for editing for “You Can See Everything” and Ludwig Göransson for music score for “The Odyssey.” “Backrooms” could surprise in production design, with Danny Vermette ahead of Donald Graham Burt for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”

	If “You Can See Everything” wins both editing and documentary, pay attention. A documentary competing in a category usually owned by narrative films would strengthen the argument that it belongs in the larger best picture discussion.

body:
Gayle King‘s son-in-law Virgil Miller has died at 45 following a battle with cancer.

	“CBS Mornings” executive producer Jon Tower delivered the sad news to the morning show’s staff on Friday in a memo obtained by Variety. In the note, Tower shared that Miller died “over the Thanksgiving holiday” following a “courageous battle with cancer.”

	Further details about Miller’s illness were not disclosed. King will take a week off from “CBS Mornings” to “help with family matters,” Tower wrote, as private arrangements are being made. The TV anchor is expected to return the week of Dec. 7.
	

	“Our thoughts right now are with her daughter, and their two beautiful children,” Tower’s memo continues. “We’re respecting the family and giving them privacy as they get through this difficult time.”

	In December 2020, Miller married King’s daughter, Kirby Bumpus, in a private ceremony at King’s best friend Oprah Winfrey’s Santa Barbara home. Miller and Bumpus shared two children, son Luca, 5, and daughter Grayson, 2. King is the mother of two children, Kirby Bumpus and son William Bumpus Jr., from her marriage to ex-husband William Bumpus.

	Miller was a Florida A&M University alumnus. There, he earned a bachelor’s degree in biology and a master’s degree in public health, while becoming a prominent student leader and drum major of FAMU’s famed Marching 100. Miller served for nearly 13 years in the U.S. House of Representatives, most recently as the chief of staff for Rep. Cedric L. Richmond (of Louisiana). In 2019, Miller joined the Washington, D.C. office of Akin as a senior policy and strategy adviser, later becoming a senior adviser focused on lobbying and public policy.
	

	King regularly shares glimpses of her family life on social media, often featuring her children, their spouses and her grandchildren as they celebrate birthdays and special occasions. On Father’s Day, King posted a cute candid shot of Virgil Miller, Kirby Bumpus, William Jr., and his wife, Elise, at a World Cup game in Los Angeles after she gifted them tickets for the holiday. King regularly referred to Miller as her “fav son-in-law” in those heartfelt posts.

title: Oscar-Nominated Director Rachid Bouchareb on the Challenges of Shooting ‘Reggane’: ‘We’re Making a Period Film in the Depths of the Sahara’
description: Among the challenges facing Franco-Algerian filmmaker Rachid Bouchareb as he prepares to shoot his next feature, “Reggane,” are rebuilding a French
body:
Among the challenges facing Franco-Algerian filmmaker Rachid Bouchareb as he prepares to shoot his next feature, “Reggane,” are rebuilding a French military base in the Algerian Sahara, sourcing military vehicles dating back to the final years of French colonial rule and dressing some 2,000 extras.

	The three-time Oscar-nominated director, whose companion documentary short “Boomerang Atomic” is screening in the Ajyal Short Film Competition at the Doha Film Festival, tells Variety that the feature is now gearing up for an April 2027 shoot. “Each time, I discover that the scale of the production means preparation takes a little longer,” Bouchareb says. “We’re making a period film in the depths of the Sahara. There are surprises.”
	

	Set in 1960, two years before Algeria gained independence from France, the film follows an Algerian shepherd who dreams of becoming a fisherman but finds himself stuck on a French military base after the army requisitions him and his livestock.

	Originally slated to begin shooting in September, the period drama is in preparation across a vast stretch of the Algerian Sahara, from south-central Timimoun, to Tamanrasset in the deep south and Djanet in the southeast. Some production locations are more than 1,200 miles from the coastal capital of Algiers, necessitating particularly complex logistical planning.

	Algerian state-owned companies specializing in desert construction are working alongside the film’s art department to recreate the military base, while the Algerian army is supplying period vehicles.

	Variety can exclusively reveal that French actor Samir Guesmi (“District B13”) is attached to the project. Further casting is underway to bring together professional Algerian and French actors alongside nonprofessional performers drawn from local communities.
	

	Since Bouchareb unveiled the project to Variety last year, its financing structure has changed considerably. The feature is now financed entirely by Algerian partners, including the Ministry of Culture and Arts and the Algerian Center for Cinema Development (CADC), a public entity tasked with developing the country’s film industry. U.S.-based Cohen Media Group and Japan’s Kingyo Films are on board as co-production partners.

	“What’s most important for me, because I’m not in a hurry, is that I’m reassured that the film will be made. That’s one less source of anxiety for a filmmaker,” he says. “I haven’t had to go looking for financing here and there. Everything is secure.”

	Bouchareb’s research for “Boomerang Atomic,” which revisits France’s first atomic bomb detonation in Algeria on Feb. 13, 1960, has also shaped his approach to the feature. He intends to move between fiction and archival footage, juxtaposing official declarations with images of the people living in the Sahara.

	“It’s interesting to show these images, particularly to contradict what was being said, namely that there was no risk, that everything was fine, that they chose this place because there was nobody there,” he explains. “And then to show some faces, the few that I found, of Algerian workers at the time.”

	The documentary has already forged connections between communities affected by nuclear testing. Its presentation by the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) in Hiroshima this past August brought together members of the film’s team, survivors of the atomic bombing and attendees from French Polynesia, where France conducted 193 nuclear tests between 1966 and 1996.

	“The commemoration in Hiroshima was a really important moment,” he reflects. “All of a sudden, these memories were connected, between the survivors of Hiroshima, the Polynesians and Algeria, through the documentary.”

	With potential school and festival screenings in French Polynesia, Bouchareb is particularly moved by the documentary’s reach. “Sometimes we don’t know where our films travel,” he says. “Having brought these memories together is wonderful.”

	He recalls a similarly powerful experience touring France with his Oscar-nominated 2006 war drama “Days of Glory,” which follows North African soldiers fighting for France during World War II.
	

	“The film allowed people to say to themselves, ‘Our ancestors participated in the liberation of France and Europe. They died by the thousands. They were heroes. So my place here is legitimate,’” he recalls. “Half the room was made up of children of immigrants. I felt that they had found something.”

	The desire to tell such stories led Bouchareb to establish his own production company, 3B Productions, in 1990. “I’m very happy to produce my own films because today I can tackle any subject,” he says. “I don’t think I would have had the career I have today if I hadn’t been my own producer. It simply would have been impossible.”

	“Boomerang Atomic” has been submitted for consideration in the documentary short film category at the 2027 Academy Awards, with Bouchareb hoping to bring greater attention to this little-known chapter of history. “The Oscar qualification opens up a few more possibilities for the film,” he says. “It allows me to talk about it through the press and make it better known.”

	Bouchareb remains open to collaborating on “Reggane” with Forest Whitaker, who boarded “Boomerang Atomic” as executive producer in October. Whitaker previously starred in Bouchareb’s 2014 drama “Two Men in Town.”

	“This important documentary made an indelible impact on me and needs to be seen,” Whitaker said in a statement.

	The director is also in discussions with Goodfellas for international distribution of the feature and is particularly keen to reach audiences in France, the U.S. and Japan. Though receptive to streaming platforms giving his films a second life, Bouchareb is adamant about where that life should begin.

	“For me, first and foremost, it’s the cinema,” he says. “The movie theater is something magical.”

title: ‘Percy Jackson and the Olympians’ Star Leah Sava Jeffries on Her Idea for Annabeth’s Gray Contacts and the Big Fan Surprise Coming in the Season 3 Finale: A ‘Dream Came True’
description: SPOILER ALERT: The following story contains plot details from “I Learn How to Grow Zombies,” Season 3, Episode 3 of “Percy Jackson and the Olympian
body:
SPOILER ALERT: The following story contains plot details from “I Learn How to Grow Zombies,” Season 3, Episode 3 of “Percy Jackson and the Olympians,” now streaming on Disney+.

	Seventeen-year-old Leah Sava Jeffries carries the weight of the world on her shoulders in Season 3 of “Percy Jackson and the Olympians” — literally. The story of Atlas, a Titan burdened by the unbearable task of holding up the sky, is one of the many Greek myths that serves as the basis for a Season 3 storyline.
	

	The Season 3 premiere saw Jeffries’ Annabeth kidnapped by a human-lion-scorpion hybrid monster called a manticore and taken across the country from Percy (Walker Scobell) and Grover (Aryan Simhadri). Annabeth faces her own struggles while her friends work to rescue her, which is new for the show; the first two seasons followed the trio going on epic quests together. With Annabeth separated for much of “The Titan’s Curse” — the third book in Rick Riordan’s “Percy Jackson” series, which Season 3 is based on — Jeffries’ main scene partners now are Charlie Bushnell, who plays Luke, and Dafne Keen, who plays Artemis.

	That’s not the only way Season 3 is wading into uncharted waters. The first-ever screen interpretation of “Percy Jackson” was a pair of movies in the early 2010s based on Riordan’s first and second books. But Jeffries is keenly aware of the fact that “The Titan’s Curse” has never been adapted.



	

					Left to right: Leah Sava Jeffries as Annabeth, Walker Scobell as Percy
	



	“It’s the first time anyone has ever seen it live action instead of just reading it in the book,” she says. “I want to make sure that I’m still delivering how the description was as much as I can, but then also still giving my own little twist with it.”While dedicated readers of the “Percy Jackson” books love to see Easter eggs in the TV show, Jeffries never wants the show to be for those fans alone. She points out many viewers hadn’t read the books until Seasons 1 and 2 came out and aims to perform for that audience too — especially as someone who hadn’t even been born yet when the original novel was released in 2005, she points out.
	

	“Coming into these roles in the beginning was a tough thing because [the books] had such a big fan base already, and so many people that already knew about them before me,” Jeffries says. “It was a lot to learn from, but I’m so excited that I was able to get this role and embody the character as much as I can.”

	Jeffries says she has learned a lot from Bushnell, 22, whom she acted opposite in several key scenes in Episodes 2 and 3 this season. She recalls him checking in after fight scenes or making sure he didn’t accidentally hit her during a take.

	“He’s such a role model for people. I learned so much stuff from him. He’s just such a great person to work with as well as a scene partner,” Jeffries says. “You could just tell he loves doing what he does, and that’s such a big thing to see because even before the show has come out, with criticism, sometimes I still get in my head. But when I watch him working, his confidence and the way he goes about things, it just makes me have a brighter day, so I’m very grateful to work with him.”

	In Episode 2, Annabeth discovers that Luke has been subjected to the punishment that once burdened. Atlas, the Greek Titan: holding up the sky. She decides to takes over him, and when the weight hits her shoulders, she lets out a guttural yell that Jeffries says was hard to find — and sounds different than she remembers. “The crazy thing is that it sounds so much more high-pitched on the show. I promise you, I have videos when I had a deeper scream and it was grittier, but I think I just lost my voice at that time,” she says, adding that the outburst didn’t come naturally to her: “I’m not a screaming person. Someone can ask me right now. like, ‘Hey, scream!’ I cannot just open my mouth and be like, ‘Ahhh!’ Like, I can’t.”

	So Jeffries devised a trick. If she needs to scream on camera, she pushes against something or strengthens her core with a quick sit-up beforehand. “I will growl before, and then go,” she says. “I have to know that my voice will hit it.”

	In the show, when a character is carrying the weight of the sky, an eerie, gray haze spreads across their eyes — achieved with color contacts. That visual detail was actually Jeffries’ idea.
	

	She says she told Daphne Olive, one of the “Percy Jackson” writers, that using contacts would give more weight to the scene. “The grayness puts the strain on your eyes. It shows that you’re in this different world and this different dreaming life,” Jeffries says. Eventually, Jeffries got approval from the production to move forward with her pitch. 



	

					Left to right, top to bottom: Walker Scobell as Percy, Tamara Smart as Thalia, Leah Sava Jeffries as Annabeth
	



	In Episode 3, still stuck in the gray haze, Annabeth has a vision of herself holding onto Percy and Thalia (Tamara Smart) as they dangle over a cliff. It’s an emotional sequence — Annabeth has tears in her eyes — but Jeffries mostly recalls how awkward it was to film. On set, she was hanging off of a practically built cliff and was fitted with wires, “because obviously, they don’t want me to fall,” she says. And though Jeffries had Percy and Thalia on her mind, she didn’t have Scobell and Smart to look at. “Whenever you saw my face, they actually weren’t even there, and I wasn’t talking to them,” she says. “I was actually holding two weights while hanging over the top, which is the funniest thing ever. Everyone was staring at me. When I looked down — I always try to do my best, but — I was so nervous.”

	At the suggestion of her acting coach, Jeffries took some quiet time to concentrate before her more emotional scenes. “It was hard because I love making jokes,” she says, “but the scene came out so beautifully. I just loved it.”

	Percy and Annabeth don’t share many moments together during Season 3, with the former going on a lengthy journey to rescue the latter. But Jeffries and Scobell spent a lot of time working together on Seasons 1 and 2, so when thinking about how to develop their relationship this season, Jeffries says they just went for it.

	“It’s crazy because we really didn’t [talk], but in a good way,” she says. “I like the fact that we had our own assumptions of what it would be like, and then just see how we were going to play it on the actual day.”

	For their scenes together, the pair would just follow their instincts without a discussion for a few takes, then put their heads together to see what else they could build. “We just knew that if we were to leave it to ourselves, then it would be better when they say action,” Jeffries adds. “We were going to learn from there.”

	From Jeffries’ perspective, the best is yet to come. She says she’s especially excited to see her work with Bushnell in Episode 5 — ”The improv we did was genuinely crazy,” she says — and teases that a big surprise is coming in the Season 3 finale. 
	

	The last episode “is something that literally means so much to me because I feel like so many people have asked for it,” she says. “I know so many people who wanted to see it, and that dream came true.”

body:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for Season 2 of “The Hunting Wives,” now streaming on Netflix.

	Earlier this month, Texas shocked the nation by electing Democrats to the governorship, the U.S. Senate and several more key positions during this year’s midterm elections. But the Lone Star State’s politics have always been seen as dynamic and complicated to those in the know — like fans of “The Hunting Wives,” Netflix’s juicy, campy drama series about a group of wealthy, gun-loving and sexually fluid women from East Texas.

	“I love our show, because you see both sides of this coin, and we’re making fun of each side,” says “The Hunting Wives” star Brittany Snow about the series’ depiction of Texas politics. Co-star Malin Åkerman adds, “We’re not going to say that we had anything to do with it, but there’s all these different people saying, ‘The Hunting Wives’ had something to do with Texas going blue!’ It’s a fun little moment for us right now.”

	Åkerman plays Margo Banks, the housewives’ confident ringleader whose Republican husband Jed (Dermot Mulroney) is a favorite to become governor. But, in Season 1, her beautiful house of cards is torn apart with the arrival of Sophie (Snow), an East Coast liberal who is shocked by the dirty underbelly of her new Southern home. Margo is full of secrets that she’s intent on keeping from Sophie, and thinks she’s in the clear when the two begin falling in love (and deep, deep lust). But Season 1 ended with Sophie discovering that Margo had gotten pregnant by a teenager, Brad (George Ferrier), before having an abortion and murdering Brad’s girlfriend, Abby Jackson (Madison Wolfe), for uncovering the truth. The only saving grace for Margo is that Sophie can’t do anything with the information, because when her brother, Kyle (Michael Aaron Milligan), attempts to intimidate Sophie on Margo’s behalf, Sophie hits him with her car and kills him instantly. Now, they’re both in trouble.
		

	Because Sophie hid Kyle’s body and told no one what she did, Season 2 begins with Margo trying to get back into her good graces. Unaware that Kyle is even dead, she keeps calling his number, getting no response until a panicked Sophie uses AI to deepfake Kyle’s voice and keep the illusion up. In person, Sophie tries her best to avoid Margo, but she can’t control herself. So she uses Kyle’s voice to ask Margo whether any of their relationship was genuine. When Margo answers that it was “100% real,” not just a ploy to cover-up the murder, Sophie is finally ready to get back together. She meets Margo at the Banks’ lake house, where they have sex — which is rudely interrupted by Zelda (Dale Dickey), a woman from Margo’s past, who sneaks up and holds a gun point-blank to Margo’s head.



	

					Dale Dickey as Zelda and Cam Gigandet as Gentle John
									Courtesy of Netflix
	



	Zelda is the leader of a biker gang in Alba, Margo’s hometown. She suspects Kyle of impregnating and murdering her underage granddaughter, Ellie (Chloe Guidry), and is attacking Margo to get information about Kyle’s whereabouts. Zelda and the gang don’t believe Margo when she says she has no idea where he is until Sophie blurts out that Kyle couldn’t have killed Ellie because she killed him. Zelda pieces together that it was someone in the gang (Cam Gigandet as Gentle John) and shoots him in the head. Soon, the police show up and the gang gets shot to death. Margo and Sophie are escorted home before they can discuss what happened, and Sophie panics, worrying that Margo will tell the police what happened to Kyle. But she doesn’t. After ignoring several calls from Sophie, Margo shows up at Sophie’s apartment and forgives her — they’re even, since Margo is a murderer too.


	The two begin secretly dating again, but Jed and his staff keep Margo on a tight leash during his campaign for governor. So Sophie hatches up a plan: If Margo publicly admits that she’s had an abortion, she’ll be able to tank Jed’s campaign and leave him for Sophie while drumming up enough support and attention to maintain her wealthy lifestyle. But right before the couple is set to make a TV appearance, Jed tells Margo that he knows she killed Abby and that Sophie killed Kyle, and that she needs to be a “dutiful wife” if she wants to keep herself and her girlfriend out of prison. Margo does still confess to cheating on Jed and having an abortion on live TV, but instead of advocating for women’s rights, she calls herself a murderer and says that prayer has allowed her to find redemption. The move is received positively by Jed’s rightwing base, and Sophie freaks out. That night, she confronts Margo, who explains to Sophie that she did it to protect her and that they can never speak again. Sophie is enraged, and says that she’ll release her recording of Margo confessing to Abby’s murder unless Margo gives her $10 million. In a brief epilogue set two years later, Sophie is uber-rich but estranged from Margo. She receives a phone call from a mysterious number and only hears panicked breathing on the other end; it’s Margo, who is covered in blood.
	

	Snow and Åkerman, in one interview, and series creator Rebecca Cutter, in a separate conversation, spoke to Variety about the absolute insanity playing out in their East Texan world.

	
		Sophie begins the season in couple’s counseling with Graham (Evan Jonigkeit). What’s going through her head in those scenes? Does she actually want to work on healing her marriage, or is it just about protecting her relationship with her son?	

	Brittany Snow: When I read the first episode and realized that one of the first scenes is her having a panic attack in her car, and then she later starts hearing sounds on the phone that are not there — I realized she’s sort of losing her mind, and that embeds in her reasoning through the entire show. She’s losing her mind because she’s losing the piece that she’s addicted to, which is Margo. So he’s just trying to fix the negativity and the guilt and shame she feels. So she’s trying to save her marriage. Maybe that’ll fix it. Or maybe she’ll run away from Margot, and maybe that’ll fix it. Or maybe she’s gonna move into this tiny house. Nothing seems to be fixing this hole, so she’s in a very psychologically dark place at the beginning of this show.



	

					Evan Jonigkeit as Graham, Brittany Snow as Sophie
									Courtesy of Netflix
	



	
		Malin, what did it feel like to pick up in such a tenuous place in Margo’s relationship with Jed, where they’re performing happiness for the cameras but barely speaking at home?	

	Malin Åkerman: I don’t like when Margo’s not on top — but it is fun to play. Margo is in the doghouse. She’s not in the main mansion. She has these bikers from her past who are chasing after her brother. Everything that could go wrong is going wrong. She doesn’t have Sophie available at all. She’s not answering any of her calls, so we find her in a really tough position, and we just want her to get her power back and get back to the unapologetic, outrageous Margo.
	

	
		How did it feel when you two came back together for the first time, which both characters are obviously craving each other, but they’re still at odds?	

	Snow: The car scene in the rain was a really difficult scene because there had to be so many things at once happening. The push-pull of a toxic relationship: “Please stay in my car. I love you. I also need you to get out. Also, I killed your brother. Also, I’m gonna have a nervous breakdown.” And it’s all those levels while looking really, really terrible on my part. Like a drowned rat.

	Åkerman: I loved that that was the first scene where we see them together, because there was so much going on and there are high stakes. Hopefully people feel the same way, like, “Oh my god! Just stay! Kiss! Get together!” 

	Snow: It was a good scene. That kinetic energy that we have. The anger that I have. You trying to win me over. It’s a lot!



	
		When Margo is trying to convince Sophie to let her back into her life in the beginning, is she being any more genuine than she was in Season 1? Or is it still about needing Sophie to help her survive and stay out of prison?	

	Åkerman: I mean, Margo comes first. She’s always gonna have her own back. But I truly think that somewhere deep inside, this is the closest to a feeling of love that Margo has had for anyone. There’s something about Sophie that really draws her in, and she feels the most herself that she’s ever felt. There’s some version of true love, as well as her survival. She can’t turn that off yet because it’s not safe yet to turn it off, and she has to make sure that she’s not going to get called out. So there’s a big duality there.


	
		Where did the idea come from for the biker gang from Margo’s past?	

	Rebecca Cutter: It was reverse engineering to get Sophie and Margo back together. The biker gang is looking for Kyle, and [since he isn’t available], who can Margo go to when she’s threatened? Sophie’s the only one that knows she killed Abby. Sophie’s the only one that knows the real her. So having that threat come into her life, in the form of Zelda and the gang, sends her directly to Sophie. Then Sophie, having to interact with Margo through the AI deepfake, falls in love with her all over again and feels guilty about what she’s done. It was this perfect storm bringing them back together. The other thing of that makes their reunion possible is that Sophie has grown and changed a lot over the two seasons. She goes from being a very weak character who feels powerless in her life to being this really formidable woman who is an equal to Margo. And realizing that they’re both killers and they both have that same drive and instinct makes them fall in love all the more.



	

									Courtesy of Netflix
	





	
		Walk me through what it was like to film all the extreme highs and lows at the end of Episode 3 leading into Episode 4: We start with a sex scene where Sophie and Margo are getting out all of their pent-up frustration from their time apart, when they’re interrupted by Zelda sneaking up with a gun, which eventually leads to Sophie blurting out to them that she killed Kyle followed by a police shootout that kills Zelda and her crew.	

	Snow: That scene is nuts. That was a nuts shoot. We also didn’t know that the song that was going to be behind it all was going to be, like — [she sings an twangy, upbeat melody] — so we’re acting our asses off, screaming and crying, and then when you see the scene, you’re like, “Wow, it’s kind of funny, actually! Comical!”

	Åkerman: You just never know how it’s gonna be edited together. But shooting it was it was a lot, over the course of two or three days. A lot of emotion. Luckily, we shot the two things separately, the intimate scene when Dale Dickey’s character comes in and discovers us, and the living room scene where the shootout happens. It was probably good for us — one mindset to the other. It’s one of my favorite things that Dale Dickey gets to say, with the gun to my head. [While Margo’s head is in between Sophie’s legs, Zelda appears with a gun and says, “Well, lookee lookee what we got here.”]

	Snow: The juxtaposition of the show is really encapsulated in that scene. The comedy, the drama, the thriller.


	
		How was it shooting Sophie’s confession that she’s the one who killed Kyle?	

	Snow: I hate that scene. Because you really see how desperate Sophie is in that moment. I don’t know if any more veins in my neck and forehead could have popped out. She’s desperate, and she doesn’t know if Margo’s going to forgive her, so the fact that she does is pretty crazy.

	 Åkerman: I loved that scene. You’re brilliant in it. All the veins. I love it all. I love it all. 



	

									Courtesy of Netflix
	




	
		For most of the rest of episode, we’re left wondering if Margo tells Jed or the police the truth about what Sophie did. What do you think was going through her head in all that off-screen time? How does she decide what to do?	

	 Åkerman: It’s a lot, and but I do think that Sophie is the closest thing to family that she has after her brother. We also know that Kyle is very unhinged and unmanageable, and who knows what he may have done to Sophie if she hadn’t have run him over? She didn’t plan on it. There were a lot of factors that she had to think about. She herself is also a murderer, so she kind of understands.

	Snow: We have this in common now.

	 Åkerman: I do think it was a lot to process. But she almost wins that cat-and-mouse chase, because she goes, “Well, now I’m back on top. I get to pull the strings and call the shots.” There are a lot of different elements to why she makes the decision to come in and say, “All right, this is how it’s gonna go. Now I’ve got you under my thumb again.”

	Cutter: Margo is, above all else, a survivor and a schemer. In a very practical sense, she recognizes that Sophie has something on her, with Abby Jackson, and she has something on Sophie, with Kyle. It’s like Russia and the United States. It’s a cold war. But now we’re even, so it’s a great place for them to be.



	

					Malin Åkerman as Margo, Brittany Snow as Sophie
									COURTESY OF NETFLIX
	




	
		She has the power again, but the scene also ends in a place that’s romantic and sweet. Usually, high-pressure moments between Margo and Sophie end with a sex scene, but in this one they just hold hands and realize they’re all each other has in the world. Tell me about shooting that. 	

	Snow: Murder brought us together!

	Åkerman: Oh my God.

	Snow: Sophie’s coming from such a nervous breakdown that any forgiveness feels like such an oasis in her mind, and especially because it comes from Margo. There’s hope in that scene. When you see Kyle’s dead body [get discovered], you realize hope is never going to last long on “Hunting Wives.” But that scene puts us on the same playing field, and alludes to the idea that things are going to be OK in their weird world.
	
		Is that how it feels to you, Malin? Is this the purest their relationship has been?	

	 Åkerman: I don’t know if I’d say the purest. Afterwards, I think it gets purer. But in that moment, Margo holds onto a few other things other than loving intentions. There’s the power dynamic where she’s also deciding that this is OK, and she is now in charge. You’re not gonna call me out for killing Abby Jackson.

	Snow: Our physicality in that scene is interesting, because you’re sitting there the whole time just watching me, and I’m pacing around, doing a tap dance. You’re just like, “Dance, monkey.”

	Åkerman: But afterwards, I loved that part of filming. We love being in love. That is the closest we get to seeing what a real relationship could be like for these two. We go, “Oh my God, they might make it! They might run off into the sunset together, and everyone else gets killed off.” That’s not what happens. But we get to see a little more vulnerability from Margo, and I thought that was a lovely part of Season 2.

	Cutter: It was important to show that the relationship is more than just sex, and that there is this deeper commitment that they’re making to each other to move past this, even though it’s kind of a fucked up commitment. I remember talking in the writers’ room about how Mandy became Margo not by dwelling on the past, but by always being willing to move on, shed her skin and transform. “We’re just gonna take this drink and act like nothing ever happened.” That’s so Margo. That’s what she has to do. She cannot dwell in any past trauma. 


	
		During the one episode where things are happy and fun, what is Sophie’s moral compass saying? Margo comes from a tough world and grew up learning to hurt people if it meant protecting herself. But Sophie comes from a more sheltered background. How is she able to reckon with what she’s done? Because she has Margo’s forgiveness, does she feel like a good person again? 	

	Snow: I think she can compartmentalize in a way that’s scary, especially when it comes to her son and her family and what she wants. She sees Margot as a beacon of who she wants to be and who she wants to be with. But she still has to be a good mother, and needs to divorce Graham. So she’s wrestling with the decision to, maybe for the first time in her life, choose herself. And that feels really good to her. She’s going to take a bubble bath in the middle of the day and show up for her girlfriend and do all these things. And then it comes crashing down. 


	
		When Sophie hatches up the plan for Margo to publicly announce her abortion so she can leave Jed and be with her, is there ever a moment where Margo genuinely plans to follow through? Or was she lying when she told Sophie she’d do it?	

	 Åkerman: Yeah, I think she had a hopeful moment where she thought maybe this could be their happy ending. There was a glimmer of hope, because that’s the thing that initially attracted her to Sophie. She’s bright and smart, and Margo noticed that about her in that very first scene when we see them together at the NRA party.




	

					Malin Åkerman as Margo, Dermot Mulroney as Jed
									DANA HAWLEY/NETFLIX
	



	
		She decides to stick with Jed since he’s figured out what happened to Abby Jackson and Kyle, and essentially begins blackmailing her. So why does she still tell the world about her abortion?	

	 Åkerman: I may not have a great answer for you. I think it’s more about the suspense, because we want to believe she’s about to say this, and to give it that really great twist at the end. That was the one scene that I had a lot of trouble wrapping my head around, like, “Why would she admit that?”

	Snow: But don’t you think she’s taking her power back? Like, “You can’t cage me, Jed. I’m still gonna say what I want.”

	Åkerman: I guess you’re right. Thank you for that!

	Snow: I saw it!

	Åkerman: I like it!

	Cutter: It’s partly to mislead the audience, also because Sophie said something to her on the phone call earlier: “You could be a hero to half the country.” Margo is a very shrewd politician and understands that if she comes forward and gets ahead of it and frames it a certain way, it could actually add to her own power. She plays a card that could have backfired, but we see that it works — and I will be shocked if, someday, a Republican politician doesn’t play this card. Mark my words.


	
		What are your predictions or desires for these characters moving into Season 3? 	

	Snow: Trying to cover up another murder, which always brings them together. I mean, we leave off this season with a cliffhanger, where it’s open to the audience whether Sophie feels like she might hear Margo’s voice or maybe she doesn’t. And Margo’s covered in blood, so we get to see these women in totally different places, physically and mentally, and they’re on a level that makes them feel like equal adversaries in a lot of ways. I just hope for Sophie, in Season 3, to take a chill pill. Maybe some Xanax! To sit in her power and not be so anxious all day. I feel like it’s coming.

	Åkerman: I think so too!

	Snow: I think she’s going to own herself.



	

									Courtesy of Dana Hawley/Netflix
	




	
		You’ve said that there’s some DNA from the “Real Housewives” reality franchise in “The Hunting Wives.” Are you going to watch Bravo’s new reality show, “Small Town Trouble: Texas,” which seems to have taken some inspiration from your show?	

	Åkerman: We’re gonna have to watch.

	Snow: We’re gonna watch, and we’re gonna like it!

	Cutter: I don’t watch that much reality TV, but I think I would have to try it. Imitation is the sincerest form of flattery.

Nov 27, 2026 1:28pm PT	
	

	
		‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Soundtrack: The Best Music Moments From Haymitch Abernathy’s Prequel Movie
	
	
			


			
			
	

									©Lions Gate/Courtesy Everett Collection
	

		
	
				

	The “Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” album is an absolute behemoth befitting the blockbuster movie.

	With 29 entries ranging from in-movie needle drops and ditties written for the dystopian movie to existing songs remixed for the occasion, it’s longer than any previous “Hunger Games” soundtrack album. (“Mockingjay Part 2” leads with 19 tracks, “Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes” clocks in at 17 songs, the original “Hunger Games” logs 16, and “Catching Fire” and “Mockingjay Part 1” both have 15.)

	Noah Kahan joins Taylor Swift, Coldplay, Lorde and Olivia Rodrigo in a starry lineup of artists who have voiced the lead single for one of the franchise’s films. Kahan’s folk-Americana style blends into the rest of the soundtrack, which runs the gamut from country to indie. The soundtrack also includes songs from the movie’s stars, Mckenna Grace, Whitney Peak and Katniss Everdeen herself, Jennifer Lawrence.

	Writing lyrics for characters with lived experiences different from your own (i.e., fighting to the death in a televised cage match against other children) is no small task. Many of the “Sunrise on the Reaping” tracks capture the struggles of Haymitch Abernathy’s (Joseph Zada) games and the overarching resistance movement in Suzanne Collins’ franchise. Others are good, but could have been left on the cutting room floor (or saved for the artist’s own project).

	If listening to nearly 30 songs seems daunting, Variety picked the 12 best moments that Hunger Games fans must dive into.


			
			
	“First in Line” by Stephen Wilson Jr.
				

	I imagine this is what most District 12 tributes think when their name is called on Reaping Day. Perhaps during the Quarter Quell Games that Haymitch enters, with twice as many tributes to face, the fight to the finish is even fiercer. And let’s not forget that classic Abernathy wisdom: “Nobody ever wins the Games, period. There are survivors … there’s no winners.” Stephen Wilson Jr.’s voice has a hint of twang and enough rasp to give this song the grittiness the situation demands; the bridge’s refrain of “I’ll keep running” builds into a final repetition with a desperate cry into an edgy final chorus that hammers that “last place” refrain until the end.


		
			
			
	“The Wheel” by Lizzy McAlpine
				

	This song feels inspired by Haymitch’s (Zada) promise to Lenore Dove (Whitney Peak) that he will eventually see the sun rise on his birthday without a Reaping. It also rings of Wiress, whose mentorship centered around the idea that “all machines can be broken,” and the role the other rebellious Victors played in Katniss’ eventual success in ending the Hunger Games for good. And Lizzy McAlpine nails the right tone of rebellion here, which doesn’t hurt either. Her voice bends, rather than breaks, to steal some of this track’s lyrics, which deftly handles the shift between the angstier chorus and the arching vocals of the verses.


		
			
			
	“Dove Song” by Sydney Rose
				

	Sydney Rose clearly knows “Sunrise on the Reaping.” This is the song that perhaps most directly and accurately references the text: The mention of Lenore Dove’s geese with the birds chirping on the backing track, the boy “sent to slaughter,” the phone line the lovers speak through while Haymitch is in the Capitol, the liquor he finds respite in after the “biggest loss” that comes after thinking he had finally escaped the Arena. This song’s strength lies partly in its accuracy to the story and also in how gentle Rose’s vocals are over these lyrics, down to the devastating final line. It’s haunting, beautiful and it’s Haymitch mourning his lost love, sung with an angelic lilt to boot.


		
			
			
	“Draw You Out” by Noah Kahan
				

	This was the first song we got from the soundtrack, and while it’s good, it’s not Noah Kahan at his best — if that tells you anything about the strength of Kahan’s latest projects. That said, “Draw You Out” is beautiful and warbling, and most of all, it really nails what Haymitch must have been feeling after returning from surviving the Games only to lose his closest loved ones, too. Wrap that up with an Aaron Dessner production bow on top, and it’s the perfect song for the movie’s end credits. This song’s shining moment is its first verse. It’s beautifully wandering, and Kahan’s lyrical talent is undeniable on lines like “I’m in a song with one descendin’ note” and “I’ve been feelin’ like a wing-clipped bird.”


		
			
			
	“Favor” by Gigi Perez
				

	This track’s cinematic opening is beautiful, as are the lyrics, which poetically capture grief. I’m particularly partial to the line “Moments were stolen, put in the frame,” which lends itself to a prevalent theme throughout “Sunrise on the Reaping”: personal moments, like Haymitch’s goodbye to his family, being used for Capitol propaganda. It’s angelic, haunting and near operatic. The lyrics are succinct and effective, perfectly balanced between the “la la la” refrains and tugging on the listener’s heartstrings with lines like “Silt in the meadow, salt in your eyes.”


		
			
			
	“Half Alive” by Mckenna Grace
				

	How can you not appreciate the work of the ultimate fangirl? From her press tour looks to her franchise knowledge to her portrayal of Maysilee (and Merrilee) Donner, Mckenna Grace has been at the top of her game. It somehow only gets better, with the second verse featuring the sucker-punch lyric “I was a sister once, I carry that love closely” and the warbling, defiant vocals of a girl who won’t be bowed on the final chorus and bridge. This is a character song executed to perfection by the actor in the role, and the overlapping dialogue that concludes the track is the brutal cherry on top.


		
			
			
	“Metal Birds” by Violet Grohl
				

	This tune dances around the film’s title, with lyrics of “Open eyes are for the weeping/Let the sun rise, just for the weekend.” The haunting quality of Violet Grohl’s croon settles nicely on lyrics about Haymitch’s struggle to break the power generator in the Arena and his defiance when looking up at the “metal birds” coming to take fallen Tributes away. The vocals are patient, the lyrics are simple and poetic. There’s a dissonance in Grohl’s delivery and a gentle brutality in each line that makes this track an unassuming knockout.


		
			
			
	“Wrestle with God” by Madeline Edwards
				

	Madeline Edwards’ song echoes elements of others that I like (i.e., the Haydove spirit of “Dove Song” combined with the grit of “First in Line”). I love the concept of Haymitch going toe-to-toe with Snow in a “wrestling with god” moment. And the contrast between the growl in Edwards’ voice on the final chorus and the gentler outro is incredible. The instrumental builds behind the bridge until she finally hits the growling final chorus and takes a deserved moment to rock out, giving this song an edge that she then reins in with the outro’s soft landing.


		
			
			
	“The Old Therebefore” by Scot Greenan
				

	This District 12 ditty comes at a particularly emotional moment during the film’s final act, and it makes me cry every time. The only thing that hits harder than this rendition is the TikTok-edited version stitching it to duet Rachel Zegler’s take from “Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.” Where hers is biting, this one is solemn but equally strong. Scot Greenan’s voice bears the kind of mournful restraint the song deserves in its scene, which lends this song the perfect near-tears tension that is bound to make any listener’s eyes well up when this track plays mid-album.


		
			
			
	“Can’t Let You Go” by Carter Faith
				

	This is the darker sister song to Sydney Rose’s “Dove Song.” It’s more mournful, but it also has the beautiful references to the dove that Haymitch can’t let go. Carter Faith’s gentle twang adds to that heartachey feel with an Americana edge the “Hunger Games” franchise does so well. Faith effortlessly toes the line between classic country and lyrics that are undoubtedly rooted in “Sunrise on the Reaping.” Take a line like “I can taste you in the shine,” which nails the textual references to Haymitch’s drinking with a delightful vocal flip from Faith.


		
			
			
	“See It Coming” by Bella Kay
				

	Another song with great “Hunger Games” lore woven into the lyrics. Reading between the lines, I see parts of it as a take on what Merrilee might have said before sending Maysilee to (almost) certain death in the Arena. “Who will I be when you leave me?” as a chorus to Maysilee asking Haymitch if Merrilee will still be a twin after she dies in the Games. Bella Kay’s mournful performance makes this one what it is: sweet high notes, tense vibrato on the post-chorus, plus she goes big on the bridge with the gut-wrenching lyrics of “Who will I be when it burns down?/You and I are out of control now/I don’t know now.”


		
			
			
	“Doing the Best That I Can (Arena Mix)” by Stevie Nicks
				

	To pull an old Stevie Nicks song for this ‘70s-inspired film is, well, inspired. Borrowing from Nicks’ discography makes perfect sense, though this 1989 track doesn’t have a novel take on the franchise. But still, it works in a way that emphasizes this franchise’s timelessness. I mean, “Fate calls this fortune and fortune takes it away” is just “May the odds be ever in your favor” to a different tune. And honestly, I’d accept more from Nicks and Fleetwood Mac on the soundtrack. “Hunger Games” to the tune of “The Chain,” anyone?

body:
For the making of “Bardi,” director Tala Hadid spent over four years embedded in the Moroccan communities involved in the centuries-old tradition of the Tbourida, an equestrian ritual rooted in warfare where horsemen charge in a single line and fire their rifles in calculated alignment. Still, despite living and breathing the rituals around the horse-riding practice, the filmmaker says she feels as if she barely scratched the surface of the intricacies of that world.
	

	“Bardi” trails a brotherhood of riders who gather for the Tbourida. The documentary observes the families involved in the tradition, as well as the heartfelt relationship between young men and their animals, with Hadid keeping her camera close to the men as they mutate from their day-to-day personas to embody an almost mythical figure atop their saddle.

	Speaking with Variety out of the Doha Film Festival after having presented the film at IDFA and Marrakech, Hadid recalls her first time seeing the riders and being entranced by their stallions. “It was so impressive,” she says. “I felt shocked by what I saw. Shocked not because it was something new but because it was such a beautifully sublime image that I felt the need to ask more questions.”

	The director, who is also a photographer whose work has been shown in institutions like the Museum of Modern Art in New York City, also lensed the film. The choice helped her keep her team small and nimble as they followed the men over the years. “I started filming almost immediately,” she says. “It was a very small production, both for development and filming. We were a small crew, which is my preferred methodology when filming with real people.”
	

	“It’s a very porous border between the camera and you as a person meeting people,” she notes of her early days of forging a relationship with her subjects. “You have to be patient because you might spend a long time filming with someone and then you end up following a completely different person. It’s like being a guest at someone’s house, where you have different people coming in and out, especially because this fraternity is a broad collective with 30, 40 people, sometimes more, so it takes some time to identify who you want to film. They were all very gracious and welcoming.”

	Asked about her motivations for capturing the community and the reality of the Tbourida, Hadid says she did not come into the project with a desire to make a “sociological or journalistic film.” “I didn’t start thinking I would do a portrait of masculinity or deconstruct the masculine. I wanted to come closer and to try and understand them. I’m half-Moroccan, and this ritual is a very important pillar of Moroccan culture, but do we really know it? Can we really know anyone or any community? How well do you know your country and your culture?”

	She says those questions tied to her national identity allowed her to walk into the process with “humility” so she could learn more about the mythology and the beliefs entrenched in the horse-riding community. “I came into a terrain that was totally unknown for me, almost like an alien. I like that way of looking, when you’re invited in to really look at something. Even now, four and a half years later and after a year of editing and finishing the film, I think I only know a little bit. I think cinema, the image, is mysterious. There’s also everything else that lies outside the frame, and what’s outside the frame is as important as what’s inside it. So you never have a total view. That’s my approach to cinema: you can’t have the total panopticon view of everything.”



	

									Courtesy Doha Film Festival
	



	This understanding of the impossibility of capturing totality through the camera also manifested itself through form in “Bardi,” which plays with notions of fact and fiction as Hadid ushers her subjects into certain situations for the film. “It was another threshold in the film, this fabulation of fictional elements,” she says. “That is something that happens in the documentary encounter. People start to change when there’s a camera. People perform. I think of it as playing a game. We explored that. We played.”
	

	Hadid says that kind of play can only happen after intimacy is developed, so she only introduced it around three years into filming. She is, however, clear in saying she does not believe in the boundaries between fiction and documentary, because “from the minute you cut an image, it is no longer the real.”

	“Even when we are watching the news, it is edited, and the cut is already a choice,” she adds. “It’s a very porous relationship. There is no frontier; it is a no man’s land between the two. When there’s a camera, you capture something that is transcending a moment, and I see it almost like a fictioning—you start to create yourself and others.”

	The director recalls setting up a scene where a father tells his daughter that she can’t ride alongside her brothers. That was a recreation of a moment that had happened in real life, and that was shared with Hadid. “Yes, I asked them to repeat that moment, but the dad didn’t need to act because it was real,” she says. “It is almost like doing therapy. We were in a space where he had to tell his daughter once again that she couldn’t ride, and it was intense.”

	“I am not saying ‘Bardi’ is revolutionary, but if you don’t shake people, if you don’t shake audiences and try to do something new, you will just make the same film again and again,” she goes on. “The eye needs to be awakened. That is the goal of an artist: not to be in these binaries, to re-look at the image and allow the image to work its power.”

									Universal Pictures / A24 / Warner Bros.
	

		
	
				

	There are 44 movies that want it all.

	That’s how many titles appear on BAFTA‘s draft Entered Films List for the 2027 EE BAFTA Film Awards, with submissions across every category open to them: best film, director, screenplay and all nine craft races, right down to special visual effects. 

	There are 126 best film entries, up from 109 eligible titles a year ago. Across best film, director, the two screenplay races and the nine crafts, 213 features are in play. Count the titles entered only in specialty races such as Documentary, Animated Film or Outstanding Debut by a British Writer, Director or Producer and the list climbs to 235.
	

	The list isn’t final. Distributors and producers have until noon GMT on Monday, Nov. 30, to request amendments and the official Entered Films List arrives Friday, Dec. 4, the same day Round One voting opens. Expect a few small corrections.

	Among the list of films submitting in every category are Denis Villeneuve’s “Dune: Part Three,” Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” Emerald Fennell’s “Wuthering Heights,” Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day,” Robert Eggers’ “Werwulf,” “Project Hail Mary,” “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,” “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple” and “Peaky Blinders: The Immortal Man.”

	Also swinging in all 12 categories are the Tom Cruise-vehicle “Digger,” “Verity,” “Send Help,” “Crime 101,” “The Death of Robin Hood,” “Heart of the Beast,” “Pressure,” “Ink,” “Tenzing,” “Wicker,” “The Sheep Detectives” and “Ghosts: The Possession of Button House.”
	

	Then there’s “You Can See Everything.”

	Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary is entered in best film, director, documentary and seven of the nine craft races, including costume design and makeup and hair. What it doesn’t have is a single performance entry, and that’s because BAFTA rules deem it ineligible.

	Amanda Seyfried, who won an Emmy playing Holmes in Hulu’s “The Dropout,” returns to the role in the A24 film’s dramatized reenactments, a performance Variety currently projects to win the Oscar for supporting actress. BAFTA joins the Golden Globes and Actor Awards (formerly the SAG Awards) among awards bodies where Seyfried is ineligible for recognition. Critics Choice stands alone in deeming her eligible for supporting actress, making it the only televised stop on the precursor circuit where she can be nominated. Critics Choice Awards nomination voting is underway.

	The four performance categories have 728 entries.

	Six performers are entered four times apiece. Zendaya is submitted in lead for “Dune: Part Three,” “The Drama” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and in supporting as Helen in “The Odyssey.” Her “Drama” co-star Robert Pattinson matches her, entered in lead for that film and for “Primetime,” where he plays Chris Hansen, plus supporting turns in “Dune: Part Three” and “The Odyssey.”

	Anne Hathaway is entered in lead three times, for “The Devil Wears Prada 2,” “Mother Mary” and “Verity” andd in supporting as Penelope in “The Odyssey.” Sandra Hüller carries lead for “Rose” and supporting roles in “Project Hail Mary,” “Digger” and Paweł Pawlikowski’s “Fatherland,” where she plays Erika Mann.British stalwarts are also spread across multiple films. Stephen Graham leads “The Good Boy” and is entered in supporting for “Animol,” “Bunker” and “Peaky Blinders: The Immortal Man.” Johnny Flynn leads “The Idiot(s)” and is entered in supporting for “& Sons,” “Elsinore” and “Tenzing.”

	Eleven more performers are entered three times: Caitríona Balfe (“A Long Winter,” “Sense and Sensibility,” “Tenzing”); Javier Bardem (“The Beloved,” “Bunker,” “Dune: Part Three”); Penélope Cruz (“Bunker,” “The Invite,” “La Bola Negra”); Monica Dolan (“The Lost Children of Tuam,” “Elsinore,” “Onwards and Sideways”); Claire Foy (“The Magic Faraway Tree,” “Savage House,” “Ink”); Andrew Garfield (“The Magic Faraway Tree,” “The Uprising,” “Artificial”); Jessica Gunning (“The Christophers,” “The Magic Faraway Tree,” “Sunny Dancer”); George MacKay (“Rose of Nevada,” “& Sons,” “Sense and Sensibility”); Bella Ramsey (“Sunny Dancer,” “The Liberation,” “The Sheep Detectives”); Mark Ruffalo (“Being Heumann,” “Crime 101,” “Spider-Man: Brand New Day”); and Tramell Tillman (“Ebenezer,” “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother”).
	

	The acting races also have new voting rules.

	Casting chapter members now vote alongside the acting chapter in Rounds One and Two. The chapter vote determines the first five of 10 longlist spots in each category, while a jury selects the final five from performers ranked sixth through 15th. Each category still yields six nominees.

	Not everyone is going wide. “Masters of the Universe” enters eight of the nine craft races, skipping original score and bypasses best film, director and screenplay entirely. “The Bride” is entered in production design alone. “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” goes the other direction, entering best film with no craft, directing or writing submissions, alongside its animated and family film bids.

	The Documentary category itself lands at 67 entries. Eight of those films are also entered in best film: “Epic: Elvis Presley in Concert,” “Musk,” “Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger,” “Everest: The Other Side,” “You Can See Everything,” “Super Nature,” “Derek vs Derek” and “Everybody to Kenmure Street.”

	Outstanding British Film draws 79 entries, with the longlist expanded from 15 to 20 films. Forty-five of those titles are also entered in best film, including “Wuthering Heights,” “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple,” “The Sheep Detectives ”o“session o” “utto” “Midwinter Break” and “Sense and Sensibility.” Nominations remain at 10, with five selected by the membership and five by a jury.

	Film Not in the English Language climbs to 46 entries, and 15 of them are also competing in best film. Among them: “Kokuho,” Cristian Mungiu’s “Fjord,” “Fatherland,” “Rose,” “La Bola Negra,” “Ramayana” and “Godzilla Minus Zero.”

	Animated Film jumps from 10 entries to 15, and 11 of them are also chasing Best Film. Pixar arrives with “Toy Story 5” and “Hoppers,” alongside “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie,” “Minions & Monsters,” Laika’s “Wildwood,” Aardman’s “Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom,” “Ray Gunn,” “The Cat in the Hat” and “Goat.”

	The jury-voted Family Film category, renamed this year from Children’s & Family Film, rises from 14 to 21 entries.

	Round One voting opens Friday, Dec. 4. It closes Dec. 29 for the four acting categories and Jan. 4 for everything else. Longlists are published Jan. 7, when Round Two voting begins. Nominations are announced Jan. 19, two days before the Oscar nominations. Round Three voting runs Jan. 26 through Feb. 16, and the 80th EE BAFTA Film Awards take place Sunday, Feb. 21, in London.

              Gayle King's son-in-law, Virgil Miller, has died after a battle with cancer ... TMZ has confirmed.
      
    
              "CBS Morning" Executive Producer Jon Tower announced the news to the show's staff in an email, USA Today reports.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
              The email reportedly stated that Gayle would take a week off from the show to grieve and be with her family during this difficult time.
      

              She's expected to return to the show on Monday, December 7.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
              Miller married Gayle's daughter, Kirby Bumpus, at Oprah Winfrey's house in December 2020 ... and Gayle shared the news a few months later in early 2021.
      
    
              Kirby and Virgil shared two children ... 5-year-old Luca and 2-year-old Grayson. Gayle previously lavished praise on the couple -- calling them "such great partners" and complimenting their parenting.
      
    
              Virgil was 45.
      
    
              RIP

description:
'The Challenge' Alum Tyler Duckworth
                          Cause of Death Revealed
body:
'The Challenge' Alum Tyler Duckworth
                          Cause of Death Revealed
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 27, 2026
                            12:42 PM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              "The Challenge" star Tyler Duckworth died from a heart issue ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
              According to the North Dakota State Forensic Examiner’s Office, Tyler died from hypertensive cardiovascular disease ... and his manner of death was ruled natural.
      
    
              Hypertensive cardiovascular disease is a heart condition caused by elevated blood pressure over years or decades.
      

              As you know, Tyler died in August after being found in an overflowing bathtub. A downstairs neighbor complained of water coming through the ceiling ... and  "tried to get the water shut off" and was "not able to confirm" whether Tyler was alive.
      
    
              We were told there were no outside signs of trauma found on Tyler's body.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
              He was honored that same month at his funeral, attended by his co-stars from both "The Real World" and "The Challenge."
      
    
              Tyler made his final public appearance at a "Challenge Mania" event in Minneapolis just weeks before he died. He appeared on "The Challenge" in 2006, and won "Cutthroat" in 2010 and “Rivals” in 2011 before returning for "All Stars 2" in 2021.
      
    
              Tyler was 44 years old.
